analysis.one_liner: Ends a tax break for hardrock mining companies and uses half the revenue to clean up abandoned mines.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee and died there when the Congress ended, so the tax break for hardrock miners remained in place.
analysis.plain_summary: Hardrock mining companies that take gold, silver, copper and other minerals from public land pay no federal royalty on what they extract, and they also claim a special income tax deduction called percentage depletion — effectively a double subsidy. This bill would have ended that deduction for mines on federal mining lands and sent half the resulting tax revenue into a new trust fund to clean up abandoned mines: sealing old shafts, treating polluted drainage, and restoring streams and wildlife habitat. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would stop footing a tax deduction for mining companies that already take minerals from public land without paying royalties; and communities living with abandoned hardrock mines, whose polluted streams and damaged land would be cleaned up with a dedicated stream of revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: It would repeal the percentage depletion allowance for hardrock mines on federal mining lands, ending a write-off that lets companies deduct a set percentage of gross income from mining.

Half the added tax revenue would go into a new Abandoned Mine Reclamation Trust Fund to pay for cleaning up abandoned hardrock mine sites — sealing mine entries, treating polluted drainage, and restoring fish and wildlife habitat.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal mining lands, which would lose the percentage depletion deduction and pay more in federal taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on public lands

drawbacks.text: Half of the new revenue would have been routed into the reclamation trust fund, meaning the other half would simply go to the general treasury rather than being guaranteed for cleanup.

The reclamation fund could only be spent on abandoned sites with no continuing reclamation responsibility under existing law and no economically recoverable minerals, excluding many of the worst-polluting sites already slated for cleanup under Superfund (CERCLA) or uranium tailings programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — ending a tax break that lets mining companies deduct more than the value of minerals taken from public land — is real and its main cost falls only on the industry itself. The principal weakness is that half the reclaimed revenue would not go to cleanup at all, and the bill got no committee action, so these merits were never weighed on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on August 4, 2009, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken — the Finance Committee held no markup and the bill never reached the Senate floor.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies kept the percentage depletion tax break, and taxpayers continued to bear the cost of abandoned mine cleanup without a dedicated fund.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies kept their tax break

for.name: Sen. Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

for.name: Sens. Maria Cantwell, Dianne Feinstein, and Bernie Sanders
Senate Committee on Finance
for.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax law
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it never came to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats or the independent Senator Sanders; the bill drew no Republican cosponsors, but there is no record of an organized opposition fight because the Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, silver, copper and other mineral miners on public and patented lands)
industries.note: They would lose the percentage depletion tax deduction, raising their federal taxes on mines on federal mining lands. Because these companies already take minerals from public land without paying royalties, ending the extra tax break would reduce a long-standing public subsidy.

industries.industry: State and local communities near abandoned mine sites
industries.note: Communities suffering polluted water and damaged land from abandoned mines would gain a dedicated federal funding stream for reclamation paid for out of the new tax revenue.
